introduction-sql-vs-dynamodb.core: Relational databases model entities and use flexible joins at query time. DynamoDB is a key-value/document store that delivers single-digit-ms latency at any scale by requiring you to design tables around known access patterns, with no joins. You model the queries first and the data second.

first_principles.problem: A team ports a normalised SQL schema to DynamoDB table by table and ends up doing joins in application code.

analogy.title: A filing system built around how you search
analogy.story: Instead of one drawer per type, you file each document where you'll look for it.
analogy.breaks: Paper copies drift silently; DynamoDB needs streams or transactions to keep copies consistent.

example.title: Order lookup
flow: DynamoDB: PK=CUSTOMER#42, SK=ORDER#2026-10-01 returns order + items in one Query

check.q: Why must you know access patterns before designing a DynamoDB table?
check.a: Efficient queries only work on keys and indexes designed for them; ad-hoc queries become expensive scans.

the-primary-key-partition-vs-sort.core: Every item has a primary key: a partition key alone, or partition key + sort key. The partition key is hashed to choose a storage partition; the sort key orders items within that partition, enabling range queries (begins_with, between) over an 'item collection'.

first_principles.problem: Fetching a user's recent orders requires scanning the whole table.

analogy.title: A filing cabinet: drawer label and folder order
analogy.story: The drawer (partition key) is chosen by name; folders inside are sorted (sort key).
analogy.breaks: Drawers are fixed-size; DynamoDB splits partitions automatically as they grow.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Latest 10 October orders in one request.

check.q: What can a sort key enable that a partition key alone cannot?
check.a: Range queries and ordering within an item collection.

single-table-design-adjacency-lists.core: Single-table design stores multiple entity types in one table with generic keys (PK, SK) so related items share a partition and come back in one Query. Adjacency lists model relationships (users ↔ groups) by storing edges as items, with a GSI that inverts PK and SK for the reverse lookup.

first_principles.problem: Fetching a user, their orders and their addresses takes three separate table queries.
truths: Same-partition items return in one call.
Generic key names allow many entity types.
derivation: **Inverted GSI** (SK as PK) for reverse lookups.

analogy.title: A family photo album organised by household
analogy.story: Open one household's page to see parents, kids and pets together.
analogy.breaks: Albums are browsed visually; single-table design needs careful documentation to stay understandable.

example.title: User with orders
flow: Query PK=USER#42 → all in one call

check.q: How does an inverted GSI support many-to-many relationships?
check.a: It swaps PK and SK, so you can query edges from the other side (e.g. group → members).

gsi-overloading-one-index-to-rule-them-a.core: GSI overloading uses generic index attributes (GSI1PK, GSI1SK) whose meaning depends on the entity type, so one global secondary index serves many access patterns. It conserves the GSI limit (20 per table) and keeps related query patterns together.

first_principles.problem: Each new access pattern adds a GSI, multiplying write costs and hitting limits.
truths: Generic attributes can hold different values per entity.
derivation: Populate **per entity type** for its pattern.
**Sparse indexes**: only items with the attribute appear.

analogy.title: One reception desk serving several departments
analogy.story: The same desk handles deliveries, visitors and post, depending on what arrives.
analogy.breaks: A desk can get overwhelmed; overloaded GSIs need their partition keys to stay well distributed.

check.a: A GSI that only contains items that have the index key attributes, making it a cheap filtered view.

hot-partitions-write-sharding.core: Each partition supports roughly 3,000 RCU and 1,000 WCU. If too many requests hit one partition key (a viral post, today's date), it throttles even if table capacity is fine. Write sharding appends a suffix (KEY#0–N) to spread load, with reads gathering across shards. Adaptive capacity helps but can't fix extreme skew.

first_principles.problem: All writes for 'events today' use PK=2026-10-18 and get throttled.
derivation: **Shard** hot keys with random or calculated suffixes.
Use **calculated suffix** (hash of ID) for direct reads.

analogy.title: One checkout for a whole stadium
analogy.story: Open ten checkouts and split the queue.
analogy.breaks: Customers pick the shortest queue; DynamoDB needs you to assign shards in code.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: 10× write ceiling for the hot key.

code.text:
import random
shard = random.randint(0, 9)
table.put_item(Item={'PK': f'DAY#2026-10-18#{shard}', 'SK': event_id, ...})
# reads: query shards 0-9 in parallel and merge

check.q: Why can a table throttle even with plenty of total capacity?
check.a: One partition key can exceed its partition's throughput limit regardless of overall table capacity.

capacity-math-wcu-rcu.core: In provisioned mode, 1 WCU = one write/sec of up to 1 KB; 1 RCU = one strongly consistent read/sec of up to 4 KB (or two eventually consistent). Transactions cost double. On-demand bills per request and scales automatically, which is good for spiky or unknown traffic; provisioned with auto scaling is cheaper for steady load.

first_principles.problem: A team can't estimate DynamoDB cost or why item size doubled the bill.

analogy.title: Postage priced by weight bands
analogy.story: A 1.1 KB letter pays for two stamps.
analogy.breaks: Post offices round to fixed bands; DynamoDB rounds per item per request.

check.q: How many WCUs does writing a 3.5 KB item once per second need?

dynamodb-streams-the-change-log.core: DynamoDB Streams captures item-level changes (insert, modify, remove) in order per item, retained for 24 hours, with optional old and new images. Lambda or Kinesis consumers react to changes: maintaining aggregates, replicating, sending notifications or feeding search and analytics, without touching the write path.

first_principles.problem: After every order write, the app also updates counters and search indexes inline, slowing requests and failing partially.
truths: Changes can be captured as an ordered log.
derivation: Use **Kinesis Data Streams** for longer retention.

analogy.title: A newsroom wire feed
analogy.story: Every change is broadcast; desks subscribe and react independently.
analogy.breaks: News is consumed once; stream records may be delivered more than once on retry.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Writes stay fast; search stays in sync.

check.q: How long are DynamoDB Streams records retained?

transactions-and-conditional-writes.core: Conditional writes apply a put, update or delete only if an expression holds (attribute_not_exists, version = :v), enabling optimistic locking and uniqueness. TransactWriteItems groups up to 100 actions across items and tables atomically (all or nothing) at twice the capacity cost.

first_principles.problem: Two requests both create the same username, or a transfer debits one account without crediting the other.
truths: Concurrent writers can overwrite each other.
Conditions check state at write time.

analogy.title: 'Only sign if the document still says version 3'
analogy.story: If someone changed it since you read it, start again.
analogy.breaks: Signatures are manual; conditional writes check in microseconds at the storage node.

check.q: How do you enforce uniqueness on a non-key attribute in DynamoDB?
check.a: Write a separate item keyed by that value with attribute_not_exists in the same transaction.
